newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish police investigate claim of Dublin abortion.
newsitem.headline: Irish police investigate claim of Dublin abortion.

text.p: Irish police said on Friday that they were investigating a claim that an abortion was carried out in Dublin in contravention of the country's Roman Catholic constitution.
Police confirmed newspaper reports that they were questioning people in connection with a claim by a Dublin woman that she was given a pregnancy termination in the capital two years ago.
Health Minister Michael Noonan said he became aware of the reported abortion, one of the most controversial issues in Ireland, two days ago but declined to comment while police were investigating.
"It would be inappropriate," Noonan told Irish radio. He said that a file was being sent to the Director of Public Prosecutions.
The case grabbed the front pages of the Irish media and threatened to reopen one of the most divisive debates in Irish history.
A 1992 referendum upheld abortion's illegal status under the Irish constitution. It can only be carried out if the life of the woman is in danger.
Pro-Life movements seized on the case to call for a new referendum to close all loopholes to abortion, which they see as a crime against humanity and Roman Catholic teaching.

But laws have been eased to allow doctors to refer women with unwanted pregnancies to clinics overseas, notably in Britain where abortion is more freely available and does not carry the same social stigma.
The alleged case came to light when a Dublin woman complained to police that she was suffering medical complications from a termination in a Dublin clinic.
By her account, carried in Irish media, she went to the clinic with an unwanted pregnancy in 1995 and was told she could have an abortion either in Britain, where it is legal, or in Dublin.
She chose to have the operation in Dublin and subsequently developed medical complications which, two years later, forced her to complain to police.
A record number of women are going to Britain for abortions, according to family planning agencies, and clinics offering "advice" advertise in Irish magazines.

The case came to light 24 hours after separated Irish couples were allowed for the first time to file for divorce after a 1995 referendum which split the country, scraping by on a majority of less than one percent.
The law allowing couples to re-marry came into effect on Thursday and the first legal divorces are expected to be granted in court by the end of March.
